1:
Henry sets the frame the others assume. Josiah had been told that the ruin of Jerusalem could not be prevented and that he himself would only be spared the sight of it, yet he did not sit down in despair because he could not do all he would; he would do his duty and leave the event to God. Who the prophets at the assembly were is disputed. Delitzsch suggests Jeremiah and Zedekiah among them, and gives Josiah a purpose in summoning them, that they might afterwards press the covenant duties on the people by their preaching; Wesley offers Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Urijah, or the sons of the prophets; Ellicott takes them for members of a prophetic order which by then formed a distinct class, and dismisses the Targum's scribes as naming a class that hardly existed so early. Delitzsch and Ellicott both note that Chronicles has Levites instead.

Who actually read the book divides them four ways, and Clarke notices how odd the question is. The high priest, the scribes, the priests and the prophets are all gathered, he says, and yet the king reads; it is strange that the high priest, or some prophet certainly present, did not read the sacred book, and he concludes that Josiah considered himself a mediator between God and the people. Henry takes the same fact as exemplary rather than strange: Josiah thought it not below him to be a reader, any more than Solomon to be a preacher, or David a door-keeper in the house of God. Wesley repeats him almost word for word, adding that all people are concerned to know the scripture and all in authority to spread it. Ellicott will not commit, allowing it was perhaps the king himself but not necessarily, since what a man does by another he does by himself. Delitzsch answers flatly the other way: he read means he had it read, that duty having devolved upon the priests as keepers of the law.

The pillar and the people's assent are smaller matters. Clarke and Gill agree that the pillar was the brazen scaffold Solomon made, on which kings were accustomed to stand, Clarke rendering it upon the stairs or pulpit; Ellicott calls it the stand or dais. On the clause that all the people stood to the covenant, Delitzsch rejects the reading that they stood firm or continued in it, holding instead that they entered into it; Ellicott says the same, that they took the king's pledge, and Henry that they signified consent and promised to abide by it, while Wesley adds that they possibly declared it by standing up as the king had stood. Ellicott alone pauses over the scale, calling all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem a natural hyperbole, since the temple court would not contain the entire population.

Clarke sets out the covenant in two parts, a general undertaking to walk after Jehovah, have no gods besides him and take his law for the rule of their conduct, and a particular one to bend their whole heart and soul to its observance, so that they might not only have religion without but piety within. Henry reads the same terms and draws three political conclusions from the scene: that parliaments are no diminution to the honour and power of good princes but a great support to them; that it is really the interest of princes to promote the knowledge of the scriptures in their dominions, a people resolved to obey by law making a kingdom happy under a prince who governs by law; and that it is no abridgment of the liberty even of princes to be in bonds to God. He adds that it is of good use to oblige ourselves to our duty with all possible solemnity, especially after notorious backslidings, since an honest mind does not shrink from positive engagements.
4:
Henry opens with two things he cannot get over: that so many wicked things should have got in and kept standing so long, when Josiah had reigned eighteen years and set the people a good example, and that despite so thorough a riddance Jerusalem was destroyed within a few years, since the generality of the people hated to be reformed. On the priests of the second order Gill and Delitzsch differ outright. Gill offers the second course, or the two chief priests next the high priest from the lines of Eleazar and Ithamar, and the Targum's Sagan, a deputy of the high priest; Delitzsch takes them for the common priests as distinguished from the high priest, and says the Rabbins are wrong in making them vicars of the high priest, which is the very explanation Gill passes on.

The black-robed priests produce the best philology. Henry takes the name as black men, or those who wore black, connecting it with the mourning garments of those who sacrificed to Osiris or wept for Tammuz. Clarke says frankly that who these were is not well known, notes that the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic call them simply the priests, and derives the word from a root meaning to be scorched or made dark, their business being to attend the fires. Ellicott disputes the black derivations on a ground nobody else raises: priests wore white throughout the ancient world except on special occasions, so it is questionable whether the term means black-robed at all. He records that Gesenius keeps the root for black but explains it as one clad in black, a mourner and so a priest, and proposes his own derivation from a root meaning to weave, giving weaver of spells, since magic was an invariable concomitant of false worship.

Two names get worried over. Tophet gets three etymologies: Henry's from a word for drum, because drums were beaten at the burning of the children so their shrieks might not be heard; Ellicott's first, the burning place or hearth; and Ellicott's preferred, that the Hebrew has been so modified as to suggest a word meaning to spit, so the name itself calls the place an abomination. He adds that Hinnom may plausibly mean shrieking, which would make the valley of the sons of shrieking a good name for the spot. On whether Baal and the sun are one deity Ellicott follows the versions in supplying an and between them, then turns on a critic who had called the Hebrew historians' knowledge of the Semitic worships very superficial, since Baal and the sun are the same: in the Assyrian system they were distinct deities, so the charge rebounds on the man who made it.

The horses of the sun draw out the imaginative and the technical. Henry canvasses that they were led out in pomp each morning to meet the rising sun, or that worshippers rode them, and concludes they drew the chariots of the sun; he marvels that men with the written word among them should conform their religion to the poetical fiction of the sun's chariot, as though the sun needed horses who rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race, when a little philosophy would have shamed them out of it. Ellicott supplies the classical evidence for such processions and for horses sacrificed to the sun, and makes a point from the wording: the chariots were burnt where the horses were only taken away, a distinction that would make no sense had the whole been one work of art in bronze, as some have supposed. On the deposed country priests Henry and Ellicott agree that they were barred from the altar but allowed the bread, Henry adding that it was better than they deserved and doubting whether they had a blemished priest's full rights, Ellicott that they ate apart and were probably put to the temple's inferior duties.
15:
How a high place of stone could be burnt only Ellicott asks. He wonders whether it was wooden, as one critic supposed, and answers with a guess from the ground: perhaps it resembled a dolmen, of which many hundred have been found in Palestine, and fire was kindled under it to crack the huge slabs, so the fragments might be crushed more easily. Delitzsch says simply that Josiah burned the buildings and ground to powder everything made of stone or metal. On what was no longer there three agree, and the agreement is an argument from silence. Ellicott observes that no mention is made of the chief object of worship at Bethel, the golden bullock, and takes the omission as indirectly confirming the prophet who foretold it would be carried to Assyria; Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion, that the calf had been removed by the Assyrians and supplanted by idols of Baal and Astarte; Wesley puts it briefly, that the calf it seems was gone, but Josiah would leave no remains of that idolatry. Wesley alone asks how a king of Judah could act at Bethel at all, and supposes the city had long been added to Judah, others having put themselves under her protection after the ten tribes were carried away.

The account of Josiah turning himself is defective, and the two handle it differently. Clarke notices that the verse is much more complete in the Greek and a Syriac version, and prints what they add, that Jeroboam stood by the altar at the feast, and that Josiah, turning about, cast his eyes on the sepulchre of the man of God. Ellicott agrees that words have fallen out and explains how: a transcriber's eye wandered from the first occurrence of the man of God to the second. He adds that the tombs Josiah caught sight of were on the hill-side opposite, not on the hill where the high place stood.

The monument draws a characteristic performance from Gill. He makes it a high and large tomb with an inscription, more remarkable than the rest, which caught the king's eye; reports the Jewish tradition that nettles and thistles grew on one side of the grave and sweet herbs on the other, and disowns it at once as not to be depended on; then keeps what he thinks may be right, that the old prophet who had asked to be buried with the man of God also ordered a pillar raised over them, which later generations maintained, so that the bones of both were saved from the fire. Delitzsch describes it more plainly as a stone erected upon the grave, and notes that the reprieve covered the old prophet out of Samaria as well as the man from Judah.

In what sense the passover was unequalled is the last question. Clarke insists the words apply not to the number present but to the manner and spirit: no passover was kept on purer principles, more heartily joined in, or more religiously observed. Wesley gives the same answer with reasons, the solemn care and great preparation and numerous sacrifices, and a joy made greater by the memory of Manasseh and Amon and the hope of a settled nation and religion. Ellicott is more exact, that no passover since the Judges had been celebrated in such strict conformity to the law, and specifies what that means, the offerings over and above the paschal lamb and the strict unity of the place; he treats the two verses as a parenthesis emphasising the phrase about the book of the covenant. He also brushes aside a critic who assumed no passover was ever held before, an opinion he says is obsolete even among advanced critics and does not merit serious discussion. Gill contributes the chronology, that Josiah must have begun very early in the year, since all this was done by the fourteenth of Nisan.
25:
That no king was like Josiah sits awkwardly beside the same said of Hezekiah, and the four who notice it handle it differently. Gill allows that Hezekiah might excel him in some things and he Hezekiah in others. Henry distributes the superlatives, Hezekiah a nonsuch for faith and dependence upon God in straits, Josiah a nonsuch for sincerity and zeal in a work of reformation. Clarke will not rank him below David: perhaps no king since David, and morally considered, David included, none so exemplary in his own conduct or so thoroughly zealous, for David was a greater but not a better man than Josiah. Ellicott declines to press the difficulty, since a writer would not measure his words by strict proportion in such a case, while granting that the Mosaic law was not so rigorously carried out by any preceding king; and he adds from the prophet that Josiah's merits did not consist merely in ritual observance, since he is praised for his righteousness as a judge.

Why the wrath did not turn is answered four ways, Henry's being an argument backwards from a promise. Since the prophet says that if a doomed nation turn from evil God will repent of the punishment, and it was not repented of, Henry concludes that the people, though they submitted to Josiah's power, never imbibed his principles: they were turned by force and kept their affection for their idols. Wesley reaches the same place from the prophets' complaints and from what happened the moment Josiah was gone, when princes and people returned greedily to their old abominations. Clarke is blunt: it was of no use to try this fickle and radically depraved people longer, and they were respited merely during Josiah's life. Delitzsch notices instead that the Hebrew makes a word-play, the Lord turned not answering to the king who turned to the Lord.

Who the king of Assyria was divides them. Clarke names Nabopolassar, and Wesley explains the title: the king of Babylon, having rebelled against the Assyrian and then conquered him, is called the Assyrian because he was now head of that empire. Ellicott reopens it: the assumption that the expedition was against the ruler of what had been the Assyrian empire holds only if Nineveh had already fallen, and on the chronology he prefers it had not, so Necho marched against a king of Assyria in the strict sense; he dates its fall to about 607, since Assyria is absent from the prophet's list of nations in 606.

Whether Josiah should have fought divides Henry from Ellicott completely. Ellicott gives a political motive without comment, that he went probably as a vassal of Assyria, resenting a trespass on territory he regarded as his own. Henry will not justify him: he had no clear call to the war, nor do we find he asked counsel of God; what had he to do to act as ally to the king of Assyria, or love those that hate the Lord? On the promise that he should come to his grave in peace, Henry reports that some think it unperformed, forfeited by his miscarriage, but holds it fulfilled, since Josiah died at peace with God and his conscience and never saw the destruction, though the providence was still a rebuke to his rashness: God has promised to keep us in all our ways, but if we go out of our way we throw ourselves out of his protection. On the death Clarke and Ellicott agree he was not killed outright, Clarke insisting the word is a participle, dying, Ellicott that Chronicles has him wounded by archers and carried dying to Jerusalem. Ellicott draws a further inference from the battlefield: that Megiddo was the meeting place shows Necho had not marched up through southern Palestine but come by sea and landed at Accho, or Josiah need not have gone so far north.
31:
Why the people passed over the elder son is agreed, and Clarke proves it from the numbers: Jehoahaz was twenty-three and reigned three months, while the brother who replaced him was twenty-five, so Eliakim was the elder, and Jehoahaz was probably raised by the people as of a more active and martial spirit. Henry adds the motive, that the people looked for someone likely to avenge Josiah's death, being more solicitous about that point of honour than about keeping up his reformation, and the issue was accordingly. Delitzsch agrees that those who preferred him had set great hopes upon him, expecting his strength and energy to avert the danger from Necho, while Ellicott had already remarked that the estimate proved fallacious. Gill identifies him with the Shallum of the prophet; Delitzsch adds what that name means, to whom it is requited, and calls the substitution significant.

On the young lion of the prophet's lamentation Henry and Delitzsch use the same image for different purposes. Henry makes it the content of the man's wickedness, that he learned to catch the prey and devour men, and that this was the evil he did in the sight of the Lord, before the nations heard of him and took him in their pit and brought him with chains into Egypt. Delitzsch takes it as evidence of character instead, ascribing to Jehoahaz the disposition of a tyrant given to acts of violence, and notes that Josephus describes him in similar terms. Henry observes that his reign was too short for his own character to show, so what is recorded is really the character of the patterns he had chosen, and draws the moral that it is of great consequence whom young people choose to imitate, an error there being fatal.

The account of the deposition carries a textual crux and Delitzsch uses it to make a point about method. Where the Hebrew says Necho put him in fetters at Riblah when he had become king at Jerusalem, Chronicles says he deposed him at Jerusalem, and the Masoretes offered a marginal reading meaning away from being king. Two critics prefer that reading because the Greek supports it in both books; Delitzsch answers that they ought not to appeal to the second passage, since the Greek there does not render the Hebrew of Chronicles but repeats the words already translated in Kings, so the supposed second witness is the first over again. On the tribute Henry notes the reversal, that formerly the Israelites had spoiled the Egyptians and now the Egyptians spoil Israel, and that what made the king poor did not make him good, since he went on doing evil under the very rebukes of providence.

The change of name draws Henry's sharpest observation. The king of Egypt, having used his power to make a king, showed it further by renaming him, and the name he chose has reference to Jehovah, which shows he had no design to make him renounce or forget the religion of his country: all people will walk in the name of their God, and let him do so. Henry sets against this the king of Babylon, who did not deal so with those whose names he changed. He notices too that the crown of Judah had until now always descended from father to son and never from one brother to another, once in the house of Ahab but never in the house of David. He closes with the reflection the whole chapter has been building towards, that a little time and slender abilities often suffice to undo the good which pious men have laboured for years to effect, though the good work which God begins by his regenerating Spirit cannot be done away, but withstands all changes and temptations.
